item.title: World’s Energy Order Tested Again as Iran War’s Reach Extends Further
item.description:
The intensifying war in the Middle East threatens to further strain a weary energy industry that has already endured waves of disruptions and could test a market resilience built on a series of extraordinary government and private-sector measures.

Over the weekend, the Iranian-backed Houthi militia attacked an international airport in Saudi Arabia’s capital, Riyadh, including one strike that killed at least 12 people and injured hundreds. It was the deadliest attack in a Gulf Arab country since the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran began in February and brought the war to the center of the Middle East’s oil industry.

The attack forced the temporary suspension of operations at the airport just as energy executives and government officials were set to arrive in Riyadh for a major business and policy conference. The event, the World ⁠Petroleum Congress, proceeded as planned, although some attendees were diverted to other airports and others, including the U.S. energy secretary, Chris Wright, and ministers from Italy and Japan, addressed the conference by video link.

Many oil industry leaders — including the chief executives of Exxon Mobil and BP — canceled their trips to Saudi Arabia, according to two industry officials who were not authorized to discuss executive schedules.

In remarks on Monday, Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman, the Saudi energy minister, acknowledged that recent attacks had “tested our infrastructure, our institutions, our people and our resilience.”

Meanwhile, oil tankers are facing persistent peril while attempting to transit the Strait of Hormuz — the narrow passage between Iran and Oman that was a fairly uncomplicated excursion before the war. At least 16 vessels have been attacked this month.

The widening of the fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthi militia in Yemen, amid no public signs of a diplomatic resolution between the United States and Iran, underscores the potent two-front threat facing energy infrastructure in an area crucial to global supplies of crude oil and its many byproducts like diesel and gasoline.

Just last month, oil exports from the region started increasing to nearly their prewar levels. More ships were getting out of the Strait of Hormuz, close to the Oman coast, through the protection and guidance of U.S. forces.

It is not yet clear if the most recent attacks on tankers around the strait will cause a notable drop in exports as ship operators recoil from the risk. Regardless, the U.S. military effort is a costly endeavor that experts say can’t last forever.

Before the Riyadh airport came under attack, an Iranian-backed militia in Iraq had already targeted a critical Saudi pipeline, which the kingdom was using to export oil instead of going through the Strait of Hormuz.

All told, the rebound in crude exports masks headwinds that could keep prices elevated, oil executives and analysts say. The benchmark global oil price was trading at about $104 a barrel on Monday, up from just under $70 on the eve of the war.

“We are in a permanently changed energy world right now,” said David L. Goldwyn, a former State Department energy envoy. “We are entering an age of prolonged insecurity.”

And the world’s crude cushions are being drained. The use of reserves of unrefined petroleum held by oil producers and governments has helped stabilize the market. Dozens of countries came together in March for the largest-ever coordinated release of stockpiles. But those reserves are beginning to have limited effect, in part because the world’s capacity to refine oil is stretched to the max.

The price of diesel has become a global flashpoint. Diesel is essential to global commerce, and a dearth of refineries has driven its price to record highs in many parts of the world, including the United States. Facing political pressure, President Trump has allowed imports of diesel from Russia, undercutting American sanctions for a measure that experts say will have a negligible impact on global prices.

The world’s reserves have reached “scarily thin” levels, Amin Nasser, the chief executive of Aramco, Saudi Arabia’s national oil company, said at the Energy Intelligence Forum in London last week.

In another potential weight on the energy market, there are signs that China, the world’s biggest buyer of oil, is starting to buy more again. Earlier in the war, China had slashed its imports to, at the lowest point, around 7.1 million barrels a day from about 11.6 million barrels.

And Iranian crude — 90 percent of which once went to China — has virtually disappeared from the market since the United States imposed a naval blockade on the country’s exports.

Oil executives say they expect the turmoil in the oil market to last well into next year if not longer.

“I think it is ⁠going to be bedlam for the bulk of the end of the year and maybe 2027,” Tengku Muhammad Taufik, the chief executive of Petronas, Malaysia’s state-owned oil and gas company, said last week.

For decades, the Strait of Hormuz was the most effective commercial route to send crude east across the Indian Ocean to Asian markets. Countries like Kuwait and Iraq used it for virtually all of their oil exports, while Saudi Arabia used it for about 80 percent.

When Iran effectively blocked the strait in March, Saudi Arabia, the region’s largest producer, leaned heavily on its other door to the world: the Red Sea. Each day, it sent four million to five million barrels of oil through the 720-mile East-West Pipeline to deliver crude from eastern oil fields to the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea. From there, ships would move its oil through the Bab al-Mandab Strait to Asia.

Over the summer, the Houthi militia made that path dangerous when it threatened to effectively block any ships carrying Saudi oil. Then in September, the Houthis attacked the East-West Pipeline, forcing it to shut down temporarily.

“Ultimately, the resilience of the international system can only hold up for so long, and we’re fast moving toward that target,” said Shaikh Nawaf S. Al-Sabah, the deputy chairman and chief executive of the Kuwait Petroleum Corporation.

Mr. Al-Sabah said that before the war, Kuwait was exporting about 2.6 million barrels a day. Production has recovered to about two million barrels a day, about 75 percent of prewar levels, because more tankers are taking the risk of transiting the Strait of Hormuz.

Also notable was the warp speed at which Saudi Arabia worked to fix the East-West Pipeline after it was damaged. Mr. Nasser said Aramco had more than 10 teams, each with thousands of contractors and engineers, that repaired pumping stations in a matter of days.

Yet the region clearly remains heavily exposed.

“Producers still need a safer route, they need tankers, they still need buyers who are willing to accept the risk,” said Aaron Brady, vice president of energy oil market services at S&P Global, a research firm, at an S&P energy briefing in London this month.

Mr. Brady added, “A lot of oil is getting out in the Middle East, but there’s no longer that sort of secure workaround.”

The bottom line, Mr. Brady said, is that even though oil is getting to the countries that want it, the routes are more complicated and the costs continue to rise. He called it an “improvised” system.

“The flows are improving, but I wouldn’t characterize this as a normally operating system,” he said.

item.title: 1 Rider Dies and Several Others Are Injured on a Georgia Roller Coaster
item.description:
One rider died and several others were injured on Monday on a roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia, the police said.

The Cobb County Police Department said in a statement that the episode happened at 3:58 p.m. at the amusement park in Austell, Ga., about 17 miles west of Atlanta.

Details about how the rider died, as well as the number of people injured and their conditions, were not immediately available.

A Six Flags representative said in a statement that park officials and the local authorities had responded immediately, but declined to describe what happened, citing the family’s privacy.

“We are deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today,” the representative said. “Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with the guest’s family, friends and loved ones.”

The representative also declined to say which roller coaster was involved.

Christina Morales contributed reporting.

This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

item.title: How Two Crypto Billionaires Are Making British Politics More American
item.description:
For a pub-going, cigarette-puffing man of the people, Nigel Farage, the leader of the Reform U.K. party, sure has some very rich friends. And two of them keep sending him and his party great gobs of money.

The gobs are so great, in fact, that the money has become Britain’s political scandal of the year. Driven by disclosures in the country’s Farage-obsessed news media, the tale has all the makings of a Netflix-worthy dramedy, one starring a pair of low-profile billionaires who rarely speak and a pinstriped populist who won’t stop talking.

That populist is Mr. Farage, 62, a jovial and polarizing scrapper who achieved national eminence as a champion of Brexit. His nativist zeal — he once claimed he was two hours late for a rally because he was stuck in traffic caused by foreigners — is matched only, it seems, by his yearning for wealth. In 2023, he was paid 1.5 million pounds (about $1.86 million) to appear on the reality TV show “I’m a Celebrity … Get Me Out of Here.” (He came in third.) He’s also a highly paid brand ambassador for a London gold dealer, Direct Bullion.

But these paydays were modest compared with the £5 million (about $6.3 million) that Mr. Farage pocketed in April 2024, when he was campaigning for the party as a private citizen. It was an “unconditional gift,” Mr. Farage would later explain, from a grateful Brexit supporter named Christopher Harborne, a British-born crypto investor who lives in Thailand, where he’s known as Chakrit Sakunkrit. In a rare interview with The Telegraph in April, Mr. Harborne said he “wasn’t expecting anything in return” for the money.

This arched some eyebrows. Mr. Harborne is worth roughly $24 billion, The Sunday Times estimates, most of it from a well-timed investment in Tether, the company behind the dollar-pegged stablecoin USDT. In June, The Guardian revealed that Mr. Farage had landed a meeting with the governor of the Bank of England and urged him to drop plans for a digital pound, known as Britcoin.

Were it issued, Britcoin would compete with Tether. Maybe there was some pro quo for all that quid.

Today, Mr. Farage is under investigation by the Parliamentary Commissioner for Standards for failing to report Mr. Harborne’s £5 million gift. He says he’s done nothing wrong. The gift was just the start of his troubles.

In early September, Channel 4 aired secretly recorded footage of senior Reform figures, including Mr. Farage, appearing to discuss ways to evade Britain’s ban on overseas campaign funding. (In one video, Mr. Farage drinks wine, eats oysters and praises polls purported to be paid for by a wealthy American donor.) A few days later, London’s Metropolitan Police opened an investigation into possible breaches of election law.

A Reform insider complained to the BBC that the party was starting to look “a bit like a pirate ship.” If that was the problem, one ardent supporter devised a curious corrective: more booty.

On Sept. 11 news broke that Ben Delo, another crypto billionaire and a self-described “maths geek,” gave Reform the equivalent of $48.7 million, the largest single political donation in U.K. history. As he explained in an opinion piece published in The Telegraph, he wanted to help Reform turn into a credible governing party.

Mr. Harborne apparently felt one-upped. The following day, he sent Reform $48.7 million of his own.

“My competitive spirit inspired me to match it,” he wrote, also in The Telegraph, “so that is what I’ve done.”

The donations caused face-palms all over Britain, where there are no super PACs and where parties receive limited public funding for parliamentary work and policy development, not campaigns. The whole system operates on a shoestring compared with the United States. Consider: In Britain’s last general election, the candidates from every party, in every constituency, spent a combined total of $125 million, said Sam Power, a lecturer at the University of Bristol, who studies political finance and corruption.

That’s about what the campaigns spent in Montana’s 2024 Senate race.

“We are seeing an increasing Americanization of the way in which people are financing politics in the U.K., and we kind of point to the U.S. as the system of worst practices,” Dr. Power said. “It’s not necessarily a Reform problem. It’s a system problem. And it has focused minds into asking, is this actually the way we want British democracy to go?”

In just two days, Reform was deluged with enough money to transform the arithmetic of British politics. And nearly every shilling came from opaque fortunes made abroad, courtesy of a donor base that could fit in a phone booth.

Britain is not the only country where politics is being reshaped by crypto. In the United States, crypto companies and their billionaire backers have emerged as a bruising new force, rewarding candidates of both parties who support industry-friendly rules and punishing those who don’t. President Trump, who once dinged crypto as “highly volatile and based on thin air” has had a conversion. In the first year of his second term, he reported more than $1.4 billion in income from his family’s cryptocurrency businesses, much of it from his $TRUMP memecoin.

Mr. Farage declined through a representative to speak for this article, as did Mr. Delo and Mr. Harborne. But Mr. Farage has styled himself as a Thames-side Trump, a grinning combatant at war with legacy finance, status quo politics and the mainstream media.

At first glance, he seems an unlikely crypto fan. He is obsessed with borders and nothing ignores borders quite like digital assets. It’s odd, too, that he favors El Salvador-based Tether over a homegrown alternative that has “Brit” right in the name.

But crypto is consonant with his image as a fearless outsider and a scourge of the establishment. It’s part of a persona he has been fine-tuning since his middle-class upbringing in the Kentish countryside, the son of an alcoholic stockbroker who left the family when Nigel was 5.

He skipped college and worked in the City, London’s financial district, as a less-than-successful metals trader, says Michael Crick, author of “One Party After Another: The Disruptive Life of Nigel Farage.” Then he served for more than 20 years as member of the European Parliament,

which was a cushy gig, but not one that pays anything close to the salaries in finance.

“He does love the trappings of prosperity,” Mr. Crick said, “and of course he has this huge resentment that he devoted his life to politics.”

In recent months, a pattern has emerged. Mr. Farage mixes money and politics and a public relations disaster ensues. After the Parliamentary Commissioner opened an inquiry into Mr. Harborne’s undisclosed £5 million gift, Mr. Farage promptly quit his seat representing the faded resort town of Clacton-on-Sea. He then announced he would run again for the same job.

“The people of Clacton can decide whether they back me,” he said in a video statement, “or whether they back the establishment.”

The establishment shrugged. None of the major parties fielded a candidate and Mr. Farage’s only real opponent was Count Binface, a comedian wearing a trash can on his head and claiming intergalactic origins.

Though Mr. Farage easily won, that summer sideshow wounded Reform. Then came Channel 4, which broadcast what was essentially a sting operation by Verbatim, a self-described investigative organization. In one of the surreptitiously recorded videos, an actor posing as an American benefactor discussed with Mr. Farage opinion polls measuring support for British parties that Channel 4 says were commissioned by Reform but paid for by a U.S. company. If the polls were an overseas-funded benefit accepted by the party, that could breach Britain’s political-donation rules

“Amazing,” Mr. Farage said of the polls. “Bang for buck.”

He later said he hadn’t been listening to that part of the conversation. Two senior aides stepped down after the broadcast. Reform has denied wrongdoing, and an internal inquiry found that the aides, not the party, commissioned the polls.

After the by-election and the Channel 4 report, Reform’s popularity started dropping. Labour’s numbers went up, propelled by the elevation of Andy Burnham, the former Greater Manchester mayor, to prime minister.

So for Reform, the noisy arrival of roughly $100 million was well-timed It changed the subject from “Reform is hurt” to “Reform is rich.”

With the windfall came a risk. Mr. Farage says his party is the voice of “ordinary people.” There’s nothing ordinary about the two billionaires now bankrolling the party.

Both have spent much of their careers overseas, though Mr. Delo said he has returned to Britain specifically so that he can give Reform as much money as he wants. To Ben Habib, a former deputy leader of Reform and now a critic of Mr. Farage, catering to rich émigrés is no better than catering to poor immigrants.

“None of the policies that Farage makes, with the exception of perhaps crypto, will have any impact on these guys,” Mr. Habib said. “And yet they’re crafting the direction of travel for British politics and the way our country is governed. And I find that really unhealthy.”

For men so politically consequential, Mr. Harborne and Mr. Delo are barely visible.

Much of what’s publicly known about Mr. Harborne comes from a defamation complaint he filed in 2024 against The Wall Street Journal over a story that he said falsely implicated him in efforts by cryptocurrency firms to mislead banks. A former McKinsey consultant, he moved to Thailand in the 1990s and founded an aviation-fuel business.

Most of his money originated from transactions that started with a fiasco and ended with a fortune. He was trading on Bitfinex, one of the world’s largest crypto currency exchanges, when it was hacked in 2016. Customers were compensated with dollar-denominated BFX tokens, which many sold. Mr. Harborne saw an opportunity and bought. He converted the tokens into equity and, through subsequent transactions, acquired roughly 12 percent of Tether.

Tether is now valued at $183 billion and Mr. Harborne owns roughly 12 percent of it. In his defamation suit, which both sides agreed to end in July. Mr. Harborne said he’s never had a management position with Tether.

“He just happened to be at the center of something massive at a very opportune time,” said Carol Alexander, a professor of finance at the University of Sussex. “It was very risky and it could have gone either way.”

Mr. Harborne has little social media presence and seems never to have submitted to a long interview or appeared on a podcast. One of the rare recordings of his voice is the snippet of a presentation he gave at his Thai resort, Kamalaya.

“One of the things we try to help all of our guests at Kamalaya is change one thing, on each visit,” he says, seated at a table, wearing a button-down shirt and sounding exceedingly chilled out. “Just one thing.”

Mr. Harborne came to his apparent serenity well into middle age. In a video clip described by The Guardian, he told listeners at a Kamalaya talk that in his late 40s, he’d worked 18-hour days, one after another, fueled by chocolate milk and cookies. Around that time, a two-seater plane he was piloting crashed into the garden of a couple in Hampshire, England. The couple were unscathed. Mr. Harborne was airlifted to a hospital with serious head injuries.

His politics are not easy to label. There’s not a peep in his opinion piece about borders or immigration. Instead, he says his main concerns are artificial intelligence, nuclear war and climate change. As for the £5 million gift, he says that the idea was born in 2019 after witnessing a protester toss a banana milkshake at Mr. Farage at a campaign stop in Newcastle.

The affront led to his resolve to “support Nigel’s security not just now, but for the rest of his life,” Mr. Harborne told The Telegraph in April. When the gift became public, Mr. Farage told a talk radio show that he might spend the money to protect himself. Or not.

“With all due respect, what’s it got to do with you?” he asked the interviewer, a bit indignantly, when asked about his plans for the cash. “I can spend it on Ferraris if I want.”

Mr. Delo grew up in Oxford, where he was tossed out of three primary schools, The Telegraph reported. (In one, his offense was vandalizing the teachers’ toilets.) At age 11, he was diagnosed with Asperger’s, a form of autism, which he said made it hard for him to read social cues. Or maybe he likes making mischief. At a formal dinner at Oxford, from which he graduated in 2005, he once wore a wet suit under his gown, The Times of London reported. The rules said that a suit was required, but didn’t offer more specifics.

He’s routinely described in the British media as the country’s youngest self-made billionaire. Whatever his net worth, which is not an easy number to pin down, his path to riches included one very public setback.

After moving to Hong Kong to work for J.P. Morgan, he co-founded BitMEX, a platform for trading crypto derivatives, in 2014. Six years later, U.S. prosecutors charged him and his co-founders with willfully failing to establish adequate anti-money-laundering and customer-identification controls. In February 2022, Mr. Delo pleaded guilty to one count of violating the Bank Secrecy Act and agreed to pay a $10 million fine. Four months later, he was sentenced to 30 months of probation.

In March 2025, President Trump issued him a full pardon.

“A legal wrong has been righted today,” Mr. Delo said in a statement. “I’m pleased to have cleared my name and to be able to continue my life and philanthropic work without the burden of an unfounded conviction.”

Mr. Delo has since been on a philanthropic spree. He’s reportedly spent more than $100 million on a variety of charitable causes, from autism to his Oxford alma mater. His standout venture is known as the Sanctuary, a cross between a WeWork space and private members club, located in a neo-Gothic building a few steps from Westminster Abbey. There is no sign on the door and those admitted are asked not to post images of the interior.

“It has Chesterfield sofas, old tapestries depicting medieval scenes, Champagne, a Fabergé egg, a taxidermy penguin,” said Harry Shukman of Hope Not Hate, a British investigative group, who has researched the Sanctuary. “It also has maps of St. Helena, the island on which Napoleon was exiled.”

The Sanctuary hosts anti-woke and right-leaning thinkers, podcasters and politicians. Among the politicians is Rupert Lowe, the founder of Restore Britain, a party that has positioned itself as a harder-right alternative to Reform.

“I think he’s concerned about the direction that Britain is taking, and that he’s doing his bit to try and change that in the way in which he judges it to be best,” Mr. Lowe said of Mr. Delo in a phone interview. “I think he’s a very good man.”

In his opinion piece, Mr. Delo said he was “out of the crypto business” and wasn’t donating in the hopes of getting even richer. His passion is the destruction of political correctness, which he once described as a “totalising ideology that’s actually strangling our societies.”

Reform, it seems, is the only party equipped to fight this amorphous enemy. In his opinion piece, Mr. Delo likened the party to a start-up outmatched by entrenched rivals that have been around for hundreds of years.

“One of the reasons why the old parties have lasted so long is that they have made it very expensive to challenge them,” he wrote. “I want a fair fight and a level playing field.”

The playing field might now tilt the other way. The party plans to hire as many as 400 campaign managers for targeted seats across the country. Mr. Farage also said he wants to build “the best research and policy operation British politics has ever seen.”

That presumes that Reform is able to keep the money.

In March, Labour introduced legislation that would cap political donations from Britons living overseas, and from those newly returned to the country, at £100,000 a year. The law would backdate these restrictions to March 25 and lead to the mother of all clawbacks. If Mr. Delo and Mr. Harborne lived overseas before that March deadline, Reform might have to return virtually all of the £72 million.

Which is why the whereabouts of these men is a pressing national matter.

“We just know that they have complied with the rules and regulations,” Richard Tice, Reform’s deputy leader, said in a BBC interview, “both existing and proposed.”

The legislation is on track to pass the House of Lords in the coming months, but the fate of the crypto bounty may well end up in court. Win or lose, Mr. Farage will cement his place as Britain’s leading populist, the local face of an ethnonationalist movement surging across Europe.

First, he might need to run for his seat in Clacton yet again. A report by the Parliamentary Commissioner is reportedly imminent, and an adverse decision could lead to a recall petition. Mr. Farage would then have to run a third time for same job. Should he win, a formidable task awaits — convincing voters across the country that he and Reform are ready for power.

“There’s no doubt this scandal stuff has damaged him,” said Alastair Campbell, a podcaster and the press secretary for former Prime Minister Tony Blair of the Labour Party. “But he’s hoping that he can be a bit like Trump, that it’s sort of priced in, it’s built in. That people will say ‘Yeah, Nigel’s a character, but let’s be honest, they’re all corrupt.’”

item.title: The Forces Driving Up Bond Yields Take a Troubling Turn
item.description:
Analysts have attributed much of the rise in government bond yields this year to inflationary pressures from the war in Iran and the bullish growth expectations tied to the build-out of artificial intelligence infrastructure.

The rising yields, they say, reflect expectations that the Federal Reserve will keep interest rates elevated to tamp down inflation from higher oil prices and prevent the economy from overheating from the A.I. build out.

But those analysts say there is a new driver of higher yields, and it is sending more troubling signals.

That driver is called the “term premium,” which accounts for the extra return investors want to be paid for the risk of lending to the government. And based on the moves in the Treasury market, those risks are rising. Last week, the term premium reached its highest level in more than a decade, reflecting investors’ growing concerns about mounting government debts, rising deficits and other fiscal challenges around the world.

Mostly regarded as an obscure concept from the bond market, the term premium is now having a real-word impact.

Investors’ demand for a higher term premium is driving up yields on Treasuries, which influence interest rates on a range of consumer and corporate debt.

Here is what you need to know about it.

Loosely speaking, there are three main factors that determine government bond yields: the expected level of interest rates set by the Federal Reserve; inflation expectations; and a final, more fuzzy category to account for the additional yield that is not explainable by economic expectations. This is term premium.

A number of factors get lumped into term premium, including but not limited to investor demand to own Treasuries, investors’ perception of the risk of lending to the U.S. government, the ease of buying and selling the government’s debt, and the likelihood that the market will swing sharply higher or lower.

Term premium is estimated by various models produced by banks, economists and others. Based on the Federal Reserve’s preferred measure, term premium ended last week at 0.9 percent of the overall 10-year yield, which stands at 5.24 percent.

And that rise in term premium has helped push overall yields higher, even as growth and inflation expectations have held steady. This measure of term premium last week reached its highest level since 2014.

Analysts said the recent moves point, in part, to a slow global reckoning, as governments that have built up huge debts have started to come under pressure from bond investors to rein in spending and reduce the amount they borrow.

In Europe, these concerns have come to the fore as France battles a fiscal crisis, with worries over its government finances helping to push the country’s 10-year note to 4.85 percent on Tuesday, roughly a percentage point higher from just three months ago. In Britain, the country’s 10-year note has climbed about half a percentage point, to 5.4 percent, over the same period. And in Germany, the 10-year note has also risen roughly 0.5 percentage points.

Investors have also become increasingly concerned about debts at home. Foreign central banks have already been shedding Treasuries for years, helping push up yields. More recently, analysts said, the government has had to compete for capital with a spate of borrowing from big technology companies, also pushing yields higher.

Analysts also said the Iran war had underscored a perception among investors that the world had become less predictable, with higher yields also reflecting an added “uncertainty premium.”

“Growth has been the story for the full year,” said George Goncalves, head of U.S. macro strategy at MUFG Securities. “The last bit has been about fiscal worries and global markets becoming a concern.”

The factors behind rising yields matter greatly to companies, investors and the government.

Some factors come with ancillary benefits.

A rise in yields driven by the prospect that the Federal Reserve will raise rates in response to higher growth implies that some companies will have increased profits stemming from that higher growth. Those profits help offset the impact of higher interest rates for companies and help keep stock values high.

Similarly, for the government, a rise in yields stemming from higher growth can help offset worries about rising deficits, with the higher interest costs balanced against higher tax revenues and a growing economy.

But an increase driven simply by investors who are demanding higher returns only weighs on the market.

Analysts at Barclays noted that “a rise in term premium raises the government’s financing cost without automatically improving the revenue base or the economy’s capacity to service the debt.”

item.title: How Climate Change Is Causing ‘the Gentrification of Seafood’
item.description:
David Leck, who buys the oysters for Elliott’s Oyster House in Seattle, loves the mellow finish of Baywater Sweet oysters and the metallic tang of tiny Olympias, but he’s most partial to oysters he remembers from growing up.

His parents used to drive him a few hours west to Hood Canal, where he would harvest them from the beach and shuck them with a screwdriver.

“There were so many oysters out in the places where now they’re so scarce,” he said. “You couldn’t walk without oysters everywhere.”

His family also dug for clams, threw out crab pots and fished for salmon, but you can’t really live that way now, he said. Summers are warmer. More people are going after fewer fish and shellfish.

With crabs, clams and oysters, you have to be more careful than you used to about bacteria and toxic algae that can make you sick, so harvest times are more limited. It’s safer to buy shellfish from restaurants and farmers who test for health hazards. But, that’s gotten pricey. Oysters that were $1 apiece not so long ago are now $4.50.

Growing up, he could never have imagined the world of the highbrow oysters where he works. “It’s crazy the shift of it all,” Mr. Leck said.

Stroll through nearby Pike Place Market and you’ll find that many once-everyday fillets and crab claws have become prohibitively expensive. In 2016, Alaska red king crab in Seattle markets fetched $25 to $45 per pound, but a marine heat wave began soon after that in Bristol Bay, where crabs were already in decline, leading to a crash in the population. Today, the crab, which has not yet recovered, retails for as much as $150 to $160 a pound.

Whole Washington Dungeness crab in 2016 was $8 to $13 a pound. Warmer water contributed to a rash of crab die-offs, and warm water related algae blooms can also shut down crab fishing. Those crabs now average $25 a pound. King salmon populations in Alaska’s famous Copper River have been falling for almost 20 years, in part because of heat-related stresses. Over the summer, a single 25-pound fish from those waters cost $2,000.

Seafood prices have never been stable. Forces like inflation, geopolitical tensions, regulation changes, international market shifts, fuel and labor costs always fluctuate. But over the last 20 years, climate change-related phenomena have added steady pulses of volatility. A pattern of disruption from droughts, heat domes, marine heat waves, sea ice anomalies, ocean acidification, atmospheric rivers and toxic algae blooms has upended the rhythms of most commercial seafood species in the Pacific Northwest.

That’s changing how people eat, with many weeknight food items becoming just occasional splurges, if not entirely unaffordable.

“It’s just amazing how expensive what used to be, you know, just a sort of run-of-the-mill food has become,” said Langdon Cook, an author and wild food educator.

Mr. Cook, who has lived in Seattle for more than 35 years, teaches foraging and cooking classes. He has watched recreational harvest seasons for Puget Sound shrimp and Dungeness crab shrink as wildlife managers seek to preserve them.

Scarcity changes how people see foods and the experience of harvesting them, he said. Take oysters. Bar patrons used to pay a dollar to slurp a shooter composed of a shucked oyster, a splash of vodka and a squirt of cocktail sauce. Now, servers point out the intricacies of oyster shells and describe “merroir,” the marine equivalent of “terroir,” as if they are fine wines.

High seafood prices inspire a kind of reverence, causing people to notice how special wild foods are, which isn’t all bad, he said. He fly-fishes for wild steelhead, which have experienced declines linked in part to warmer ocean temperatures. They’re delicious, but he’d never keep any now, he said. He wants every single one to reproduce.

“There are just certain foods that are no longer on our plates.” he said. “Maybe you could call that the ultimate reverence — foods that we don’t eat any longer.”

Many aspects of Seattle life have become more expensive with the influx of high-earning tech workers who have relocated there for companies like Amazon, beginning in the 2010s.

“You do have people with quite a lot of expendable income. So going out and eating a dozen oysters for an appetizer and spending 60 bucks plus two drinks before you have dinner, isn’t a big deal,” said Lauren McCool, an oyster educator and shucker with Pop Up Oyster Bar. “But I don’t. I don’t love how inaccessible I feel like they’ve become.”

Mark Kurlansky is a Connecticut-born journalist who wrote “Cod: A Biography of the Fish that Changed the World” and other books about fisheries. He thinks often about the shifting place of seafood in culture and the consequences for fishermen.

“What is it? The gentrification of seafood?” he said.

The phenomenon of once-abundant fish becoming expensive isn’t limited to the Pacific Northwest, Mr. Kurlansky said. Atlantic cod, for example, used to be a blue-collar food. When, as a boy, he asked his mother what was for dinner, she’d say halibut or flounder, but if it was cod, she’d just say “fish.”

But since then, Atlantic cod was aggressively overfished to the point that fishing ceased for decades in order to let the population recover. It never fully did. Now warm ocean temperatures stress the remaining fish.

“The fact that a cod is a delicacy is a huge cultural shift,” Mr. Kurlansky said. “I mean, a cod was such an ordinary fish.”

Fishing drives economies and preserves communities, he said, but it has become harder to sustain.

“If we’re telling fishermen that they should catch less fish, they have to earn a living,” he said. “So how do you earn a living catching less fish? You make more money. The prices have to be up. That’s the only way it’ll work.

“So, you know, if you can do that, then what do poor people eat? Does seafood just become something only for rich people?”

Pacific Northwest oysters, even with their increased price, might be a bright spot when it comes to resilience in the era of warming seas. The region is a commercial powerhouse in the U.S. oyster farming industry, and has also become a hub for innovating ways to combat the effects of climate change.

For example, when ocean acidification, a result of rising levels of carbon dioxide, began causing oyster larva die-offs in the late 2000s, farmers and scientists developed water monitoring systems, began spawning larvae in less vulnerable off-site locations and used buffering treatments to stabilize production.

Another problem is vibrio, naturally occurring bacteria that can make people sick. In summer months, it has always been a problem because warmer air and water temperatures promote the bacteria’s growth. Extremely warm summers, like the record-breaking one in 2015, can make that worse.

Lissa Monberg is a co-owner of Hama Hama Oyster Company, on Hood Canal, where her family has been farming oysters for a century. The company has now invested in depuration tanks that flush the bacteria from the oysters, and for more than a decade, has operated farms in several locations, so if one area is shut down, there will be another source for customers. That has helped with another problem that’s grown worse in recent years: toxic algae.

Since last summer, a new marine heat wave off the West Coast has pushed temperatures 3 to 4 degrees above normal, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. Warmer water spurs the growth of Alexandrium, a type of algae that can cause paralytic shellfish poisoning, which is potentially fatal to humans. Oysters, crabs and other shellfish filter the water, concentrating the toxin.

Over the summer, the Washington State Department of Health shut down all recreational and commercial oyster harvests across Hood Canal because of an algae bloom, only the second major canal shutdown in Hama Hama’s history. The last widespread shutdown occurred during another marine heat wave in 2015, but was shorter in duration, Ms. Monberg said. This one impacted business from June to August, she said.

They were able to continue selling oysters from safe beaches elsewhere. Diverse locations have become a selling point, because oyster flavors vary by place and customers like the variety. But each location increases operating costs.

“It’s capital intensive and it’s complex,” Ms. Monberg said. “I think it’s true of farming everywhere. I know, any farmer would say that as the environment becomes less predictable, you have to have backup plans to your backup plans.”

Alice and Van Helker started Fjordlux oysters, a small farm in Hood Canal, a few years before the pandemic. Both have a background in biology and saw oysters as a sustainable seafood, with a positive impact on water quality and a low carbon footprint. The pandemic years, a summer where a heat dome baked oysters on the beach and the recent algae-related closure have been curveballs.

“There’s been so much stuff that I didn’t know to plan for that I didn’t even know to think about,” Ms. Helker said.

Farming isn’t easy, especially since they became parents, but there’s still a robust market for oysters in restaurants. They have also been selling oysters directly to customers at a local farmers’ market, which is one of the more affordable ways to get them.

Even with the risks, farming still feels worth it. “Oyster farmers and shellfish farmers are super, super-dedicated people. Like, we want to do this work,” she said.

The rising cost of fish and shellfish also spurs innovation in Seattle kitchens. Becky Selengut, a Seattle-based cookbook author and private chef, uses Dungeness crab far differently than she used to. “I’ll extract the meat and use it as a garnish and use the shell for a stock,” she said. “I’ll just make it last and use it in more creative ways.”

She also buys salmon whole, which is cheaper, and uses all the parts, preparing off-cuts like bellies and collars and crisping skin.

“You don’t need to serve everybody a pound of seafood on their plate,” she said. “Four ounces is plenty for most people.”

Some people say there’s reason to stop eating wild local seafood altogether, but Ms. Selengut is not convinced.

“Here’s the other philosophy from my friend who’s a fisherman who fishes in Alaska: She says you have to eat it to save it, right?” she said. “You have to have it be part of your life and part of everyone’s life in order to have the advocacy around it to keep it going.”
